analysis.one_liner: Bans senior Pentagon officials and generals from working for defense contractors for two years after leaving.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Armed Services Committee without ever getting a vote, despite the sponsor and 40 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred two groups — senior civilian officials of the Department of Defense and retired generals and Navy flag officers — from taking pay from a defense contractor during the two years after they left government service. Existing federal civil penalties would apply to violations, and officials could ask in advance whether the ban covered their situation. The bill was referred to the House Armed Services Committee and sent to a subcommittee, but no vote was ever scheduled and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who fund defense contracts. The two-year waiting period is meant to slow the revolving door through which senior defense officials and retired generals move straight into defense companies — the firms they recently oversaw or negotiated with — which is widely seen as inflating procurement costs and skewing contract decisions toward contractors' interests.

how_it_helps.text: Bars former senior civilian DOD officials from accepting compensation from a contractor for two years after separation, and applies the same two-year bar to retired generals and Navy flag officers [S2][S3].

Defines a 'senior civilian official' as anyone in a position paid at or above the Senior Executive Service minimum rate, so the ban reaches the top civilian ranks, not just political appointees [S2][S3].

Makes existing federal civil penalties apply to violations and lets a covered person request official advice on whether the ban applies to their situation, so the rule is enforceable and predictable [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Senior defense officials and retired generals and flag officers, who would lose two years of immediate high-paying contractor work after leaving the Pentagon. Defense contractors would lose direct access to those recent decision-makers as hires and consultants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Defense contractors and departing senior officials

drawbacks.text: A two-year employment bar can discourage experienced senior officials and officers from leaving active service at all, or push talent out of government entirely, since they cannot immediately use their skills in the private sector [S2][S3].

Defense contractors and some officials argue that recently departed leaders hold genuine technical expertise that industry and even the government benefit from, and that the ban covers people whose work posed no conflict; the bill's grandfathering provisions also leave employment arrangements begun before the effective date untouched [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost falls on a small, well-paid group of former officials and on contractors' hiring pipelines, while the benefit — cleaner defense procurement decisions and less immediate influence-peddling by recent insiders — reaches every taxpayer who pays for weapons systems. The bill was a narrow, targeted ethics rule rather than a sweeping ban, and its main weakness is that a two-year window does not address the broader culture of the defense revolving door. On balance the benefit outweighs the cost, though the bill by itself would only have trimmed one channel of contractor influence.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Armed Services Committee and referred to a subcommittee, which never acted, so it died when the two-year Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles E. Bennett of Florida introduced the bill on May 24, 1989, joined by Reps. Boxer, AuCoin, and Penny as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
Forty House Democrats cosponsored the bill [S4].
The House referred it to the Armed Services Committee the day it was introduced; three days later it went to the Subcommittee on Investigations and the Pentagon's views were requested [S5].
No subcommittee vote, committee markup, or floor action followed, and the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Senior defense officials, retired generals, and defense contractors keep the current rules, which let them move from the Pentagon into contractor jobs with only the shorter waiting periods then in federal law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Defense contractors and departing senior Pentagon officials

for.name: Rep. Charles E. Bennett
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-FL), bill sponsor and chair of the Armed Services Panel on Defense Procurement
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose a two-year cooling-off period before senior defense officials and generals could take defense contractor pay.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, referred it to the Subcommittee on Investigations, and never reported it out or scheduled any vote.

against.name: Subcommittee on Investigations
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral on May 30, 1989, with no hearings or votes recorded before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 40 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill died in a committee controlled by the Democratic majority, so the record shows Democratic sponsorship but no recorded votes to measure partisan support or opposition.

industries.note: The bill would have barred contractors from hiring or paying recently departed senior Pentagon officials and retired generals for two years, cutting off their most direct access to the people who award and oversee their contracts. Contractors' interest in hiring insider expertise runs against taxpayers who foot the bill for procurement shaped by that access.

industries.industry: Retired senior defense officials and general and flag officers
industries.note: These former officeholders would lose two years of immediate high-paying private-sector employment after leaving government, which is the price the bill placed on their insider access.
